📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

June, 1977. Cliff Booth runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, tends a couple bars, and drives a tow truck to a demolition derby. These are not his only day jobs, and they’re all at night. In his spare time, the ex-stuntman disappears blackmailers with a payoff or a bullet. Something called Star Wars has taken over theaters, threatening a half-century of blockbuster family fun. Cliff inhabits an older world, gnarly yet noble, gory and shagadelic. He runs with blaxploitation macks, bored Malibu wives, underworld assassins, the snobby former critic of the Superfood Gazette and whoever that body in the trunk used to be. These are Cliff Booth’s people — and Quentin Tarantino’s, too. Once upon a time in the 1990s, Tarantino was the breakout bad boy of independent film, surf riding the crest of a youth tsunami. Now he’s our reigning entertainer-historian, overstuffing hard-R sensations with motion picture lore. He owns the real New Beverly in actual Los Angeles. So when Netflix agreed to make his Once Upon a Time in Hollywood follow-up, they paid him a fortune to advertise his theater. Franchises have been no-brainers since, well, Star Wars. But a sequel on a streamer is something new for Tarantino. And The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth marks the first time in 30 years that someone besides him has directed one of his screenplays. Let’s get rambling to find out where it ranks in his filmography.

According to recent reports, he swears he will make only 10 films. We’re starting at 17. Is he lying, or is this list stupid? Probably both. However, this ranking seeks totality: his screenplays, his TV diversions, the simple fact that Kill Bill counts as two. Let’s count all his official writing and directing credits — plus this middling erotic thriller, which earned him a co-producer credit for doctoring the script. (He later polished Crimson Tide and The Rock.) A beautiful social worker with a bodacious lake house gets knocked up by an ex-con who maybe killed his pregnant wife. You hear trace Tarantino elements emerging in Past Midnight’s dialogue, especially when a cop says the phrase “natural born killer.” And a very minor character, the snarky physician, is named “Dr. Zastoupil.” Quentin Tarantino was Quentin Zastoupil through childhood, keeping his stepfather’s surname even after his mom’s second divorce. A teen dropout with acting ambitions, he snagged “Tarantino” back from his biological father. Not because he loved the guy, matter fact he barely knew the son of a bitch. It just sounded better.

Recent findings suggest that after Pulp Fiction won him his first Oscar, he hosted Saturday Night Live, got his head blown off in his buddy Robert Rodriguez’s Desperado, and played an animistic “god with a small g” named Johnny Destiny in the interminable Vegas comedy Destiny Turns on the Radio. Then came this dire anthology. Miramax must have hoped for generational showcase, with studio mascot Tarantino joining Rodriguez and their Sundance youngfriends Allison Anders and Alexandre Rockwell. Each filmmaker writes and directs their own Latest Year’s Eve farce, set on different floors on a Tinseltown hotel. Tarantino also stars in his entry, playing a fresh-minted shirtbird celebrity who complains if you call his Cristal mere champagne. It’s a wearisome (if admirably self-aware) snapshot of his peak overexposure, and a disastrous victory lap for the renegade age of indie cool.

The rest of Four Rooms’ band of outsiders started directing the regular independent way, with little money and amateur pluck. Anders’ and Rockwell’s first features were black-and-white cheapos about arty goofs, and Rodriguez wrote a book about El Mariachi’s $7,000 budget. Reservoir Dogs looks insanely professional by comparison: soundtrack money, a prosthetic ear, Harvey Keitel. Tarantino’s missing link is this early unfinished comedy he directed about DJ pals on a manic night out. Acolytes peg My Best Friend’s Birthday as a True Romance beta test, though the fuzzy half-hour cut online suggests an alternate timeline where he made loosey autobiographical romcoms instead of meticulous profane epics. Pompadoured with earrings like some rockabilly nerdpunk, his character plainly admits he has a foot fetish.

He owns a couple theaters, co-hosts a movie podcast, and wrote a great book of film criticism. Still, deep down, I wonder if Quentin Tarantino is more of a TV guy. His work chases an old forever feeling of channel-surfing into some random weekly episode about characters walking from place to place, meeting people, and getting into adventures. In the 1996 biography King Pulp, author Paul A. Woods memorably quotes Steve Buscemi: “When I saw Pulp Fiction, the little boy watching this big TV, being alone in the room, the TV being his friend — to me, that’s Quentin.” Does that explain why, fresh off Kill Bill’s impressive exertion, he directed a couple hours of a hit procedural he adored? Wiliam Petersen’s brainiac cop Gil Grissom reveals an abiding fandom for Roy Rogers. Frank Gorshin and Tony Curtis play themselves. George Eads’ niceguy Nick hallucinates his own autopsy while buried alive.

CSI was already half-lame by 2005. This NBC hospital drama was still blazingly cool in its first season. And while Tarantino dutifully hits CSI’s CBS marks, he brings an exuberant kick (and some cool long takes) to ER’s Mother’s Day episode. One patient is newly earless. Julianna Margulies and Sherry Stringfield lay out on the roof, barefoot and sunglassed.

Sources indicate that for one cultural millisecond, in the month between the third El Mariachi and the first Kill Bill, Rodriguez was awesomer than Tarantino. Actually, he came off like the real Tarantino: a legitimate peddler of anything-for-a-dollar gut thrills, not a devoted student expostulating the genre curriculum. Alas, Rodriguez early-adopted all the millennium’s annoying industry trends: 3D, CGI backlots, HiDef video, rigid adherence to sacred Comic-Con texts. A lot of hot shit gets fucked in his frantic adaptation of Frank Miller’s comic noir. The ensemble shot in a void; post-production filled in the cartoon cityscape. Tarantino was “Special Guest Director” for helming practically the only sequence without violence, when Clive Owen’s heroic goon drives Benicio Del Toro’s evil goon to the local tar pits. Del Toro’s already dead, which doesn’t stop him from having a very entertaining conversation. Easy to guess this greenscreen pit of hell was not Tarantino’s bag. He kept filming on film, and made celluloid his theaters’ mission statement.

Industry observers note that movies! Good for you, or bad? The first Kill Bill ornated Uma Thurman’s vengeance quest with samurai codes, Ennio Morricone needle drops, Shaw Brothers zooms, weeks of wirework, and fountains of bloodgush. When martial arts legend Sonny Chiba rhapsodizes about the sword he just made, it’s sheer religious ecstasy for a cultural obsessive. A decade earlier, director Oliver Stone adapted an early Tarantino screenplay into a screed against media obsession. Woody Harrelson and Juliette Lewis play Bonnie and Clyde plus MTV, sinners idolized into celebrities by our broken culture. Acclaimed cinematographer and psychedelic wizard Robert Richardson shot both Kill and Killers, blending multiple stocks and intense aesthetics. You don’t watch these films. You inhale.

To the straight world of 1994, Tarantino and Stone probably looked like identical madmen. There was no love lost. Tarantino disavowed Stone’s Killers and published his original script as a middle finger. Stone added activist Russell Means as a kind of shaman, declaring with moral authority that the whole problem is “too much TV.” I assume Tarantino thought Stone was a preachy boomer, and that Stone saw Tarantino as everything wrong with a Generation X. Who was right? Are we living in a dark dystopia of true-crime infotainment and mass-transmitted megalomania? Or a wonderworld of multicultural exchange, with no divisions between highbrow and lowbrow, where a “silly Caucasian girl” in Bruce Lee’s clothes becomes a feminist action hero? Actually, they both nailed it. And these Killfests only rank so low because I’m an old man who prefers 20-minute dialogues to 20-minute action scenes.

Rodriguez directed and Tarantino wrote this genre mash-up. The divide between their styles is clear as the Tex-Mex border. Dusk’s daylit first hour is pure rancid QT-inflected neo-noir. George Clooney — never meaner, never hotter — and Tarantino himself play the fugitive Gecko Brothers. Killers fatale Juliette Lewis and top Reservoir dog Harvey Keitel are RV-riding normals forced to drive the bros south to El Rey. Oddly, the fun falls off at the halfway twist, when surprise vampires lock the doors at the Titty Twister and trap the cast in a horror-comedy. Still, the closing lines pinpoint Tarantino’s unsteady moral code. “I may be a bastard,” says the last man standing, “But I’m not a fucking bastard.”.

Industry observers note that from Dusk Till Dawn also has the snake dance: Salma Hayek, wearing little except a Burmese python, pouring liquor down her leg so Tarantino can drink it off her toes. An astonishing scene, really, if you only care about desire. When he directs, Tarantino is comparatively chaste. He prefers a good flirt, with comfortable silences. He’s only filmed one sex scene — in Jackie Brown, in the kitchen, standing, 9/10ths clothed, loveless — unless you count a couple man-to-man assaults. I’m talking about sex because Grindhouse, the flop that ended his Rodriguez partnership, turned into their significant sex movie: gauzy with the male gaze, an essential artifact from the dirtbag 2000s. They each made their own film, then released them together as a three-hour double-bill. (Never watch the split-off versions. For better and worse, the three-hour experience depends on too-muchness.).

Recent findings suggest that rodriguez’s kickoff feature, Planet Terror, is the more obvious HR nightmare: Produced by then-wife Elizabeth Avellán, starring eventual girlfriend Rose McGowan as a gun-legged go-go dancer, overseen by the studio boss who wound up disgraced for assaulting multiple women (including, allegedly, McGowan.) Tarantino’s Death Proof is smarter and safer, punctuating all-female convos with car-assaults by Kurt Russell’s ladykiller stuntman. The director later told the Church of Tarantino podcast that he based Tracie Thoms’ badass driver on a girlfriend and all the women onscreen reflect genuine female posses he rolled with. I dunno. The chicks’ habits mostly evoke novelist Gillian Flynn’s immortal line that “Cool Girls are above all hot.” Lotta booze-swilling daisy-duked dames here, who dig Zatoichi and keep finding upcoming ways to put their feet up. You can’t be cynical when the climax is an act of friend-to-friend hero worship. Stuntwoman Zoë Bell was Thurman’s Kill Bill stunt double. Fascinated by her talent — and furious at the computers invading fast cinema — Tarantino cast Bell as herself to ride on top a Dodge Challenger for an all-time car chase. In her daffy stunt-action charisma, you spot the primordial Cliff Booth: genial, lusty for danger, more than a little insane.

Industry observers note that since we’ve talked about sex, we should talk about race. Spike Lee was not the only one noticing all the n-words in Tarantino’s dialogue. To love his work, you do have to kinda think cultural appropriation is a good thing, that it’s okay for anyone — even a white kid from the South Bay — to melt the cultures he adores into one major pot. That may even be the conventional wisdom; Tarantino’s biggest success is his Blackest. Jamie Foxx stars as the freedman learning the bounty trade from Christoph Waltz’s cheerful German. Tarantino won his second Oscar for a baggy script, which runs an hour longer than Sergio Corbucci’s stupendously garish Django (source of Unchained’s name and theme song). Foxx’s gunslinger is too mythic for any personality, especially compared to Leonardo DiCaprio’s plantation tyrant Calvin Candie. But Tarantino has always been interested in performance as an act of self-preservation. (Track how many people on this list go deep undercover into a life-or-death con.) Foxx comes alive when Django playacts race betrayal as a Black slaver. As the head of Candie’s household, Samuel L. Jackson gives what amounts to a ferocious double role, plotting brilliantly behind a mask of loudmouth servitude.

According to recent reports, after the Crazy 88 fight wraps the first volume on an operatic high, the deadliest woman in the world gets taken down by… Budd, a drunk with a shotgun. Tarantino regular Michael Madsen plays the ruminative assassin as the one person in the Billogy who lives anywhere close to reality. Working in an empty strip club and living alone in the desert, Budd is another proto-Cliff, a doomed killer basking in the slushy margarita of his decay. 2 is great fun — the showdown in Budd’s trailer is Tarantino’s best fight, period — until the talky finale veers baffling. Despite Thurman’s all-in performance, I’m not sure she (or anyone) can fully unpack the romantic-paternal Bill-Bride dynamic. Was the anticlimax purposeful? After months of martial arts training, David Carradine’s one significant bit of choreography is a 12-second seated swordfight. Tarantino used to promise a third volume, possibly suspecting that 2’s happy ending left unfinished business.

I love it. I love it! You’re telling me David Fincher — the serious man, the hundred-take cyborg, the serial killer fetishist — you’re telling me that David Fincher directed a plotless meander about a dude in puka shells bopping around Los Angeles? Cliff Booth looks fuzzier than Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, because digital still can’t capture night like 35mm. The obvious CGI (and alleged AI) adds to the cut-rate effect — like some high-tech toupee the whole screen is wearing. With Leonardo DiCaprio’s sadsack Rick gone, Pitt’s good-timer Cliff mixes banana margaritas, plays tennis, watch TV with his pops, and walks the earth like Caine in Kung Fu. “I’m not that deep,” he tells Elizabeth Debicki’s tall drink of Aussie. Co-star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II has a specific line, “This don’t mean shit to me,” that gets repeated a couple times. Should we trust that carefree attitude? Is this Tarantino’s Walking Tall Part 2, a low-ambition cruise backward through pleasurable familiar territory? Don’t miss the elegiac resonance. Cliff’s a gig-economy freelancer juggling six or seven jobs, scamming friends out of cash, commodifying his own buff bod, living with a gainfully employed parent. The biggest movie of 1977 is about to bankroll the rise of Industrial Light & Magic, which will do for stuntmen what ChatGPT is about to do to me. From that perspective, Cliff’s commitment to joy isn’t just infectious. Motherfucker, it’s revolutionary. (Read The Hollywood Reporter’s full review here.).

In a recent development, still his cleanest screenplay, especially when things get messy. A wild bunch of color-coded badmen congregate in a safehouse. Somebody’s dying, somebody’s lying, somebody’s crazy, and everyone’s armed. Skeptics noted similarities to Ringo Lam’s City on Fire. That Chow Yun-Fat thriller has romance, impressive heists, and a sincere cop-criminal friendship. Dogs’ robbery is unseen. The one woman is a doomed bystander. The most tender friendship aims toward oblivion. What a cast: Keitel’s gruff Mr. White, Madsen’s smirkish Mr. Blonde, Tim Roth’s gutshot Mr. Orange. Even pallid quirkster Steve Buscemi looks damn slick as Mr. Pink, nailing Tarantino’s caffeinated patter and the perfect SoCal deployment of “man” as a punctuation mark. Buscemi should have been in all these movies. At a minimum, he should have played any part Tarantino wrote for himself.

Skeptics call him ironic or nihilistic, but Tarantino does believe in good guys. The Bride, Cliff Booth, Django, and even Zoë Bell are paragons, their violence justified by righteous vengeance. Django appeared in the original concept of this snowblood frontier mystery, until Tarantino realized his white hell had no place for an iconic moral compass. Django became Major Marquis Warren, plantation-raised Union veteran, brilliant sleuth, unrepentant killer, documented Friend of Lincoln — and the greatest Tarantino character, played by the greatest actor to ever spout a Tarantino monologue. What secret does Samuel L. Jackson understand about his longtime director? Is it just a Tennessee thing: One born in Nashville, the other raised in Chattanooga? Hateful Eight traps Jackson’s disgraced veteran in a stagecoach stop with seven other tough customers. Three hours in a blizzard would feel claustrophobic, if everybody wasn’t such a riot. Kurt Russell’s noose-happy bounty hunter comes off crude and naïve. Jennifer Jason Leigh’s captive looks on, watchful and feral. Walton Goggins chatters memorably as the jerky bigot who worships a Confederate husk played by Bruce Dern. At once statelier and more bugfuck than Django, this second Western of Racism luxuriates toward its nutty-in-ever-sense twist. Make of this what you will: In the High Obama days of liberal goodwill, Tarantino made three features looking back (and ahead) toward fascism and white supremacy.

Industry observers note that yes, Christian Slater is too pretty as Clarence, a Sonny Chiba-worshipping Quentinian comics clerk. Yes, the dark nonlinear screenplay got straightened out with a happy ending. Yes, the score has a lotta marimba. No, I don’t believe a sweet call girl like Patricia Arquette’s Alabama would ever fall for a geeky john her fourth day on the job. Director Tony Scott saw something in Tarantino’s writing, though, that nobody else ever found. Met-cute and insta-wed, Clarence and Alabama flee smoky Detroit for sunny California, with stolen coke in their bag and hell following after them. Gary Oldman, Christopher Walken, and James Gandolfini are all memorable baddies, even more impressive since they all only have a scene or two. A couple detectives come off like lunatics, because they’re played by Tom Sizemore and Chris Penn, men never known for their good behavior. It all works as glossy gutter pulp, set with comic precision in the chlorinated motels and rollercoasters of Los Angeles. But Scott was a true romantic. He makes Alabama and Clarence the greatest of Tarantino’s straightforward heroes, so stupid with passion that even colliding criminal underworlds can’t stop their love. Sound like a fairy tale? Fine. Pretend it’s called Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.

1978’s The Inglorious Bastards was a rude romp about semi-psychotic soldiers in Occupied France. That’s the sort of squad-on-a-mission plot Brad Pitt’s Aldo Raine seems to be arranging in this similar-titled war film. The Lieutenant assembles eight Jewish servicemen (and one Hugo Stiglitz) to scalp a hundred Nazis apiece. But Aldo and his Basterds only show up after a lengthy opening interrogation, which introduces Waltz’s Jew-hunting Hans Landa. Then the Americans mostly disappear for a whole middle hour. The action shifts to a Paris cinema, and a basement bar. Parallel plots converge. Mélanie Laurent’s moviehouse operator seeks revenge for her murdered family. Aldo and his allies devise an attack. Goebbels (that Goebbels) hopes Der Führer (dat Führer) loves his upcoming movie. Basterds’ tavern setpiece marked a complete inversion from Kill Bill’s excess: Twenty dialogue-heavy minutes of twisted-nerve tension followed by 15 onslaught seconds. It’s the Inglourious experience in micro, full of vivid characters and fatal consequences.

Industry observers note that after Pulp Fiction, everyone knew what “Tarantinoesque” meant: Funny, shocking, loquacious, retro, now. Then he returned with a marvelous, middle-aged, low-key caper about a desperate flight attendant and a bail bondsman sick of bonding bails. “Didn’t exactly set the world on fire, did you, Jackie?” a lout detective teases the title character, who makes a piddling $16,000 plus benefits before she gets popped smuggling cash with a sprinkle of cocaine. Tarantino was casting Pam Grier for talent, not just stuntcasting her ‘70s fireball persona. When Jackie lands in jail, the soundtrack cranks the song Grier sang for the 1971 prison-hottie wackfest The Big Doll House — but the look on her face tells you the wild days were a long time ago. She finds an unlikely ally in Robert Forster’s Max Cherry, a bond agent weathered by years of scum and bureaucracy. Jackie’s big problem (and biggest opportunity) is Ordell Robbie, a gun dealer astounded at his own cleverness. Add in Robert De Niro’s semi-verbal ex-con and Bridget Fonda’s pothead siren, and you’ve got a collection of misfits in the South Bay — the former home of Quentin Zastoupil. Jackie Brown is the director at his least Tarantinoesque and most Zastoupilian, uncovering surprising soul in a landscape of food courts, airplane-hotel bars, beach pads, delusional small time crooks, and the occasional oil derrick. Transplanting Elmore Leonard’s novel from Miami, Tarantino chopped a gunfight, unrequited the romance, turned a white woman Black — and added one last ambiguous kiss.

Sources indicate that what’s your favorite chapter? The buzz in ‘94 fixated on Vincent Vega and Mia Wallace at Jack Rabbit Slim’s, that binary-star supernova of John Travolta’s comeback and Uma Thurman’s arrival. Me and my teen buddies, scared or baffled by love, preferred the middle segment, with a katana-wielding Bruce Willis. The final act of corpse disposal has the most questionable rep, depending whether you think Tarantino’s acting is serviceable or unforgivable. (He’s fine.) Yet it’s the last bit that reveals Jackson’s Jules Winnfield as Pulp’s moral core. Tarantino characters rarely change in the screenwriting-101 sense — he keeps casting Brad Pitt to specifically not do an emotional arc — but Jules is transformed after six point-blank bullets miraculously don’t execute him. In a moment of clarity, he starts wondering over Ezekiel 25:17, the Bible verse he’s been misquoting. Has he been his brother’s keeper? Or the tyranny of evil men? Heavy themes for a sensational quotefest, but Tarantino was always after more than his bratty referential imitators. His characters dress cool, talk cool, murder cool, and know cool things. It’s not enough to just be cool. So Jules becomes a killer who doesn’t kill — a Bad Mother Fucker trying real hard to be the shepherd.

Industry observers note that brad Pitt exudes folkloric chill as convertible cowboy Cliff Booth. Whereas Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton is all hat and no cattle, a whiskey-soured mess with a nervous stutter. They’re near-nobodies in Hollywood’s Hollywood: A stuntman who can’t get stunt jobs, a fading TV star clutching guest parts. One memorable day, they both go to different fake Wests. Rick’s on a backlot doing a cowboy TV pilot. Cliff returns to the defunct western town at Spahn Ranch, where lurks doom. A fatal mood lingers, even if you don’t know the history. Rick got famous on Bounty Law for never bringing back his targets alive. Cliff maybe-definitely killed his wife. Zoë Bell is the stuntlady who refuses to work with a spouse-killer — hilarious, since Kurt Russell plays her stuntman husband, and they were the stuntpeople trying to kill each other four movies ago.

That’s just one way Tarantino Voltrons together his whole filmography into his magnum opus. Here’s a Los Angeles thriller, a meta-western, and an alternate history, with Grindhouse-worthy re-enactments and a whole society incapable of turning off the radio or the television. There’s even — call Oliver Stone! — a meditation on screen violence, with one wannabe murderer declaring “If you grew up watching TV, that means you grew up watching murder!” Is it weird the heroes are older men, while the Mansonites (Margaret Qualley, Sydney Sweeney, Mikey Madison, Austin Butler, Maya Hawke) turned out to be Gen Z’s top stars this decade? I think Tarantino was being honest about late midlife fears, with Rick in particular worrying that some whole rising generation of longhairs is coming for his ass. There’s always been so much you don’t see in Tarantino’s movies, though, like Dogs’ jewelry store or Pulp’s briefcase. The climactic awe in Hollywood is how magnificently one substantial nothing happens. Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate is a luminous mystery, worshipped yet unknowable. Manson himself barely appears. Tarantino resurrects an era that finished horrifically in the true 1969, then merrily twists the facts. Sadness embeds in that fantasy. We know the end came and will come again. Celluloid projection won’t return to the global multiplex, no matter how many repertory theaters Tarantino runs. Nobody lasts forever, in Hollywood or anywhere else. Good thing art is death proof.

The $TRUMP memecoin has been in circulation for nearly two years now, with the value declining by around 99 percent since its launch in January 2025.

But fear not, investors, because Donald Trump had a surprise up his sleeve.

"Our president has a gift for grift. Over the weekend he hosted a dinner at his golf club in Virginia for all the top suckers who invested in his memecoin. It was billed as 'the most exclusive dinner in the world,' with guests Floyd Mayweather, Tristan Thompson, and Kevin O'Leary from Shark Tank," explains Jimmy Kimmel in the clip above. "It's so inspiring to see: Even while he's so busy knocking down the White House, botching the war, tanking the economy, [he] still finds time to run a pyramid scheme out of his golf course.".

Unfortunately the celebrity dinner doesn't appear to have moved the price much. $TRUMP is currently trading at around $0.81, down from an all-time-high of over $70. Still, at least it's made Trump himself some money.

Tech Report: November's full moon dazzles skywatchers with a stunning Beaver Moon supermoon (photos)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov.
  • In a recent development, each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising.
  • November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

In a recent development, each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.

November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.

Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.

Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in Upcoming York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.

Hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of Upcoming York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.

Sources indicate that our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.

According to recent reports, "Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up.".

Sources indicate that this striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.

Allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.

It has been revealed that "Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image.".

Recent findings suggest that moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?

Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.

That Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.

Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

#117081. A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1498 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them.
  • Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside. Scientists believe these mysterious objects, known as primordial black holes, could have formed during the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when extremely dense regions of matter collapsed under their own gravity. If they exist, these ancient remnants could also account for a substantial portion of dark matter, the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

It has been revealed that researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them. Using theoretical calculations and computer simulations in three dimensions, the team investigated what would happen if a primordial black hole became trapped inside a star similar to our Sun.

Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility. A black hole no larger than an atom, but carrying the mass of an asteroid, could gradually sink toward the center of a star and begin consuming it from within.

Industry observers note that if the star rotates rapidly enough, material falling toward the black hole would eventually form a spinning disk around it. That development could set the stage for a catastrophic explosion.

"Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star," states lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

Recent findings suggest that the interaction between the black hole and the surrounding disk could produce enormous jets of matter that punch through the star and cause it to explode within seconds. Researchers predict that the resulting outburst would emit intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays, potentially making it visible to telescopes already in operation.

"There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars," Gottlieb indicates. "We expect this to be visible, and it's something we should look into.".

The research team also included Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of Fresh York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University.

Ancient Black Holes That May Have Survived the Significant Bang.

Not every primordial black hole formed in the early universe would still exist today. According to a theory developed by physicist Stephen Hawking, black holes gradually lose energy through a quantum process called Hawking radiation. Over immense periods of time, this process causes them to shrink, and the smallest primordial black holes would already have evaporated completely.

Heavier primordial black holes, however, could have survived to the present day. Some might be approximately the size of an atom while containing as much mass as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

These extraordinary objects raise an intriguing question. If they are still scattered throughout the universe, what would happen when one encounters a star? More importantly, could the resulting interaction provide the evidence needed to establish that primordial black holes actually exist?

To investigate, Gottlieb and his colleagues combined mathematical calculations with numerical simulations incorporating general relativity, fluid dynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their goal was to understand how a primordial black hole could become trapped by a star and what would happen afterward.

How a Tiny Black Hole Could Become Trapped Inside a Star.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that a star acting alone generally could not capture a primordial black hole passing nearby. Its gravitational attraction would be insufficient to keep the black hole from escaping.

According to recent reports, the situation changes when another object is involved. A companion star or planet could alter the gravitational interaction enough to allow the primordial black hole to become trapped.

Industry observers note that in this arrangement involving three objects, the black hole could repeatedly travel through the star. Each passage would create friction as it moved through stellar material, gradually draining energy from its orbit and drawing it closer to the star's center.

Industry observers note that the process could take thousands or even millions of years. Although that sounds extraordinarily slow, it is relatively brief compared with the age of the universe.

Eventually, the black hole would settle into the star's core, where it could begin feeding on the surrounding material.

"Then, this is where the action begins," Gottlieb states.

A Black Hole Could Slowly Consume a Star From Within.

In a recent development, once the primordial black hole reaches the stellar core, its growth depends partly on what happens to the energy generated as gas falls toward it. Some of that energy can heat the surrounding material, potentially slowing the rate at which additional gas falls inward.

In a recent development, the team's simulations indicate that most of the energy would instead disappear into the black hole. This would allow it to accumulate matter more rapidly than earlier estimates suggested.

Over several million years, the growing black hole could consume approximately 1 percent of the star's total mass. At that stage, its fate would depend heavily on how quickly the star rotates.

According to recent reports, if the star spins fast enough, gas would no longer be able to plunge directly into the black hole. Instead, the material would gather into a rotating disk around the black hole, which would by then have grown to several meters in size.

"Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk," Gottlieb claims. "The black hole is also spinning, and it's twisting space and time.".

Industry observers note that as the disk continues feeding the black hole, the extreme rotation twists the magnetic field threading the surrounding material. This process could generate exceptionally powerful jets that shoot outward from the black hole's poles.

"This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole," Gottlieb explains. "And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It's very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.".

What began as a tiny black hole hidden inside an otherwise ordinary star could therefore end in a violent explosion, with the star's destruction unfolding in a matter of seconds once the critical conditions are reached.

Exploding Stars Could Reveal Primordial Black Holes and Dark Matter.

The researchers also calculated what these unusual explosions might look like to astronomers, estimating how their brightness and color would change across different wavelengths of light.

Their models predict a recognizable sequence of emissions, beginning with high-energy radiation and progressing through other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum as the explosion evolves. The initial outburst could include intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma rays and X-rays.

"We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions," Gottlieb says. "This is something we could potentially detect, if it's not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.".

Such signals could be detectable with existing astronomical instruments, potentially allowing researchers to search for primordial black holes far beyond the Milky Way.

Recent findings suggest that however, identifying one would not be straightforward. Other cosmic events can generate similar flashes of radiation, so an unusual explosion alone would not establish that a primordial black hole was responsible.

In a recent development, astronomers would need to examine additional evidence, including the characteristics of the exploding star. One especially revealing clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not ordinarily be expected to meet such a violent end.

It has been revealed that "For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside," Gottlieb states. "The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.".

Even if no convincing examples are found, the search could help scientists determine how common primordial black holes might be and how much dark matter they could account for.

For now, primordial black holes remain hypothetical. But the upcoming research offers astronomers a possible observational signature to pursue, connecting the spectacular destruction of stars with objects that may have existed since the universe's earliest moments.

Recent findings suggest that the research received partial support from the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program and the National Science Foundation.

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

Industry observers note that the studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

In a recent development, the tech giant plans to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz remarked on the firm's earnings call earlier this month.

According to recent reports, paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

In a recent development, the earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The company has stated it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

#117077. Industry News: A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1476 w)

Industry News: A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

Recent findings suggest that the US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

Industry observers note that as long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, notes study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

Industry observers note that the immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler stated.

It has been revealed that mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

Sources indicate that the fresh nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

According to recent reports, the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

According to recent reports, “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler mentioned.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

Industry observers note that as promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, stated Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an upgrade.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler notes they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss firm called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

In a recent development, other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a upcoming vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

According to recent reports, in reality, Poland stated, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he noted.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax states it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in Newly introduced York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team claims it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very crucial in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler stated.

Recent findings suggest that they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

Recent findings suggest that fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler mentioned, so it would have to be used carefully.

Industry News: Mysterious latest viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history.
  • Sources indicate that the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins.
  • In a recent development, the discovery could have notable implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering newly introduced clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

Sources indicate that the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the new evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

In a recent development, the discovery could have notable implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious Fresh Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection.

In a recent development, at the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

The newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

In a recent development, "What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," noted Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future.".

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences.

To uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

Rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

Industry observers note that the databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

According to recent reports, "The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically.".

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions.

Beyond identifying the newly introduced viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

According to recent reports, their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

Sources indicate that this raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past.".

Upcoming AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries.

Recent findings suggest that the research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

In a recent development, supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

It has been revealed that "If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque said. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts.".

NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.
  • Sources indicate that first to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground.
  • In a recent development, A configurable LED array, built at APL and spanning the light spectrum from the infrared to the ultraviolet, provides information about the color of surface materials at the sampling site and helps scientists make inferences about their composition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.

Sources indicate that first to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground. By mid-November, all seven cameras developed and built by Malin Space Science Systems had been installed in their insulated housings, tested, and integrated into the rotorcraft. Each camera will look out at Titan through a window in a foam enclosure that insulates the cameras and Dragonfly’s interior from Titan’s cryogenic environment, where ambient temperatures reach minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit.

In a recent development, A configurable LED array, built at APL and spanning the light spectrum from the infrared to the ultraviolet, provides information about the color of surface materials at the sampling site and helps scientists make inferences about their composition. During Titan’s long night, which spans nearly eight Earth days, these observations also may allow DragonCam to identify organic molecules that fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The LED illumination also allows us to see Titan as human eyes would.

Sources indicate that “One of the most exciting things about Dragonfly is that we'll be able to see Titan from perspectives we've never had before,” noted Elizabeth Turtle, Dragonfly principal investigator at APL. “With the capability to take images when Dragonfly is on the surface as well as while flying, DragonCam will give us both detailed views and sweeping panoramas of Titan's landscape, as well as insight into the processes that shaped this extraordinary world. Seeing these cameras become part of the Dragonfly lander is an exciting milestone that brings us another step closer to this unprecedented exploration.”.

In addition to these science cameras, Dragonfly has two navigation cameras, also built by Malin Space Science Systems, that were installed this summer.

Industry observers note that “We are extremely pleased to have delivered the DragonCam cameras,” mentioned Michael Ravine, DragonCam development manager and a Dragonfly co-investigator from Malin Space Science Systems. “Now to have them on the Dragonfly spacecraft, taking images, it’s so much easier to picture how they will work on Titan. These will be our eyes to see and explore this whole newly introduced world.”.

In a recent development, two forward-mounted cameras — a wide-angle camera (WAC) and medium-angle camera (MAC) — are designed to capture images of the terrain in front of Dragonfly. The forward WAC offers a 90-degree field of view, while the forward MAC overlaps with the WAC, capturing part of that field of view at a higher resolution. Combined, the images from these two cameras provide a stereoscopic perspective from the front of the lander. Together with two additional side-mounted WACs, the system is able to capture panoramic views of the Titan landscape.

It has been revealed that two downward-facing WACs provide views of the surface beneath Dragonfly, helping the mission team decide if a landing spot is safe for deploying Dragonfly’s sample-collecting tool, known as DrACO, or Drill for Acquisition of Complex Organics, and its seismometer. A high-resolution microscopic imager will aim at DrACO’s drill site to pick out the details in millimeter-sized sand grains around the sampling location.

“DragonCam will give us critical context for the samples collected by DrACO,” stated Carolyn Ernst, the DragonCam instrument scientist at APL. “We’ll be collecting materials at multiple sites across Titan, and the images from the cameras will help us relate the samples to Titan’s broader landscape and piece together the story of its geology.”.

Sources indicate that components of Dragonfly's other instrument packages, DraGNS (Gamma-ray and Neutron Spectrometer), DraGMet (Geophysics and Meteorology), DraMS (Mass Spectrometer) and DrACO, are set for delivery, integration and testing over the next several months. Dragonfly is scheduled to launch in July 2028 and reach Titan in late 2034.

Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.
  • The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang.
  • The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.

The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar.

The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun.

According to recent reports, quasars occur when supermassive black holes are surrounded by vast amounts of gas and dust on which they feed. The immense gravitational influence of the black hole causes this material, in the form of an accretion disk, to glow brightly and to blast out bright jets of plasma. That means quasars at the heart of galaxies in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs) like this one can often be brighter than the combined light of every star in the entire surrounding galaxy, but only briefly.

The newly discovered quasar, designated J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, is in this brief phase of its existence. It was discovered among millions of objects in 18 months of data from Euclid.

Recent findings suggest that euclid's initial observation of Dún Aonghasa was followed up by an array of ground-based and space-based telescopes, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). It was the JWST that determined the mass of this supermassive black hole.

It has been revealed that what is interesting about Dún Aonghasa is that it is unlike other supermassive black holes seen at a similar period of the early universe. That's because this black hole is feeding relatively slowly. That means if it engaged in rapid feeding to reach its massive size, that period of gorging on gas and dust has either ended or it has paused.

That is something that further complicates our picture of supermassive black hole growth.

By staring back 13.1 billion years in time to see Dún Aonghasa, Euclid is also observing a crucial time in cosmic history when the first stars and galaxies were taking shape, and the clearing of cosmic gas was ending the dark ages of our universe by allowing light to travel freely.

Recent findings suggest that euclid's primary mission is improving our understanding of dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the expansion of the universe, and dark matter, the most mysterious "stuff" in the cosmos. Collectively, these aspects of the universe account for around 95% of its matter-energy budget and have come to be collectively referred to as the dark universe. Hence Euclid's nickname as the "dark universe detective.".

This research, along with Euclid's discovery of at least 12 that date back around 13 billion years, shows that this pioneering space telescope released in 2023 could also make a major contribution to our understanding of black holes and their growth.

Sources indicate that the team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Latest Update: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • In a recent development, the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

In a recent development, the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

Sources indicate that it's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," noted Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

According to recent reports, fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves promptly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out new garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

It has been revealed that "We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," said U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

The average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," remarked Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

In a recent development, though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

Industry observers note that sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She mentioned that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

"There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman said. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

In a recent development, nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

Apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, said BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

In a recent development, "Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," mentioned Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, noted China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

Sources indicate that "They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," stated Lu.

AlixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," said BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also noted she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

According to recent reports, ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the firm remarked it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

Recent findings suggest that the brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Sources indicate that alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Sources indicate that shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky mentioned worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the organization is doing well.

Recent findings suggest that "What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," stated AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".
